items.text: An AI-led selloff hit Wall Street on Friday, Nov 20. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% to about 6,910, its seventh straight loss, and the Dow fell 1.9% (950 points) to 48,147. Both are now more than 10% below their records, which puts them in correction. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.3% to 22,618 and is now down for 2026. Reuters says Anthropic's IPO fell flat, which deepened worries about the AI trade, and Nvidia's strong results did not calm fears about heavy AI spending. Nvidia fell about 14%, AMD, Micron and Broadcom each lost 12–14%, and tech was the worst sector (-7.3%). The S&P lost 8.6% on the week, its worst week since April 2025. The VIX jumped to about 36, Treasury yields fell sharply (10-year 4.92%), gold dropped about 4.6%, and bitcoin fell below $60,000. Asian chip-heavy markets had already fallen 5–6%.
items.notes: Small differences between sources: Reuters has Nvidia -13.8% and Anthropic -9.1%; the Capp Notes wrap has -14.01% and -8.50% (Anthropic closed at $88.91, still above its $83 IPO price). Sector, VIX, yield and commodity figures come only from the Capp Notes wrap.

items.text: At a long White House news conference on Nov 20, Trump said he would 'love to see' Jensen Huang 'given a second chance' as Nvidia CEO. He called Huang a good man who made bad decisions and urged him to apologise and return. Trump also said Xi Jinping had called Huang 'brilliant' during their Shenzhen meeting. Al Jazeera notes this contradicts Treasury Secretary Bessent's account that Huang did not come up. Nvidia's board, led by chair Harvey Jones, has said it unanimously accepted Huang's resignation and does not plan to reinstate him. Trump said he still backs Commerce Secretary Lutnick, whom Sen. Tom Cotton accuses of ignoring warnings about chip smuggling to China. Democrats are looking into whether Lutnick helped Cantor Fitzgerald.
items.notes: Trump's account of Xi's remark conflicts with Bessent's, per Al Jazeera. No board response to Trump found as of Nov 21.

items.text: At the same Nov 20 news conference, Trump said US companies that build data centres in other countries would face 'tremendous penalties' or 'a tremendous tax'. He argued that 'China will take all of them' and framed the threat as part of an AI race with China. He gave no details on how a penalty would work or on its legal basis. He also said he and Xi had agreed on unspecified 'joint guardrails' for AI. US cloud and AI companies, including hyperscalers and OpenAI, are building large data-centre projects abroad, especially in the Gulf, Europe and Southeast Asia. The threat follows the Nov 19 BIS rule requiring licences for advanced chips in data centres in several Southeast Asian countries.
items.notes: A verbal threat; no executive action found. The CNBC article could not be fetched, so only the headline was seen. No company reaction found yet.

items.text: On Nov 20 Trump signed an executive order requiring federal contractors and subcontractors to notify the White House and their contracting agencies about any pending or future congressional request concerning their government work or their communications with the executive branch. They must coordinate on responses and on which privileges apply, and must withhold material the White House says is covered by executive privilege. Agencies must tell contractors about these duties. The White House says the order protects confidential and national-security information. Reuters notes that Democrats take control of both chambers in January and are expected to launch investigations of the administration. Oversight experts expect the order to be contested, but no reactions were found yet.
items.notes: The line about experts expecting a challenge is analysis, not sourced reaction. The Reuters piece quotes no lawmakers. The EO number was not confirmed.

items.text: Late on Nov 19 the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a broad permitting overhaul, by 62-33. Fifteen Democrats joined almost all Republicans. Thirty-one Democrats and Republicans Hawley and Rounds voted no. The bill changes how reviews and permits work under NEPA, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, the Historic Preservation Act and the Federal Power Act. It limits lawsuits against projects, gives FERC new authority over interstate transmission lines, and includes provisions meant to keep ordinary ratepayers from paying for power hookups to data centres. The White House backs it, and Trump claimed on Nov 20 that it would save households $1,300 a year. The Sierra Club, NRDC, 17 Democratic states and tribal groups oppose it. It goes to the House after Thanksgiving. Speaker Johnson says it can pass, but Jeffries' office says it 'falls short'.
items.notes: The vote was late on Nov 19 ET and was not in the earlier logs. Trump's $1,300 savings figure is his claim (CBS live blog). Wyden's proposed amendment banning data centres on public lands: outcome not reported.

items.text: Fed officials kept signalling a December rate hike. According to a Nov 20 market wrap, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson, a 2026 voter, said she would be open to back-to-back hikes, and Governor Lisa Cook warned that waiting longer risks falling behind the curve. Cook dissented against hiking in October. Kalshi priced a 25bp hike at the Dec 8–9 FOMC meeting at about 90%. Data released the same day were softer: the University of Michigan's final November survey showed one-year inflation expectations falling to 3.7% from 4.3% at mid-month, the lowest since March, and sentiment at 51.5. Treasury yields fell 12–13bp as investors sought safety.
items.notes: The Cook and Paulson Nov 20 remarks were not confirmed in a primary Fed transcript; the Investinglive Paulson piece may be from earlier in the week. Relevant to W-261107-01.

items.text: A Nov 20 market wrap says Reuters reported that SEC enforcement staff are examining Nvidia's accounting, and that California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office sent Nvidia an investigative subpoena over whether its chips reached China. Both were cited as reasons for the stock's roughly 14% fall. Earlier, the WSJ (Nov 17) reported a civil SEC probe into whether Nvidia's disclosures about Asia misled investors, including its ties to Singapore's Megaspeed. Bonta had told Bloomberg TV that 'red flags' had been raised and that he was weighing action.
items.notes: The subpoena and accounting-focus details were not seen in a primary Reuters or AG source; treat with caution. The SEC disclosure probe itself was reported by the WSJ on Nov 17.

items.text: In his first news conference since the midterms, back from Asia, Trump said he would veto Democratic-led bills unless Democrats work with him and would issue an 'ultimatum' later. He said he is open to working with them on healthcare, called Hakeem Jeffries 'a smart guy', and described a productive call with Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa. He brought his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, to the lectern and asked him whether he wants to run for president. He defended Vance's remark blaming the Iran war for GOP midterm losses and said he would have won had he been on the ballot. He did not lay out a plan for the Dec 11 funding deadline.
items.notes: The CNN takeaways page could not be read (robots block), so only its headline was seen. CBS did not cover funding or shutdown remarks.

items.text: Trump said at his Nov 20 news conference that National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving and that Kirsten Davies has been named to replace him, pending Senate confirmation. He also said the recent string of outages, including the FAA ground stop and the NSANet disruption, were 'all separate events'. Cairncross was confirmed in August 2025. The change comes as senators press the White House over AI-enabled cyber threats.
items.notes: Only the CBS live blog was seen; no official announcement or independent confirmation of Davies' nomination was found. Relevant to W-261118-02 and W-261114-01.

items.text: Trump said he met more than 20 leaders on his Asia trip, 'secured two new trade deals' and expects about ten more 'very soon'. He named neither deal. He said the US is 'getting close to a deal' with Mexico and working with it against cartels, and that Canada has been 'ripping us off' and is not yet satisfactory. Earlier, the Philippine ambassador said nothing had been signed with Manila despite Trump's claim of the 'biggest trade deal' ever.
items.notes: No deal texts were found. These are Trump's claims.

items.text: Trump defended his relationship with Vladimir Putin on Nov 20. He said Putin told him the Ukraine war would never have happened had Trump been president, and that the relationship gives the US 'additional strength'. Russia launched more attacks on Ukraine after the Shenzhen meetings. Trump said the joint statement with Xi and Putin covered non-proliferation, refined-petroleum supply, rejecting ICC authority and UN reform. On Iran, he said there is a 'rumor' Tehran is building a dirty bomb, which the US 'will not allow', and that he wants a 'real deal', not a 'fake' one. He also touted an almost 60-cent drop in average gasoline prices over the past month.
items.notes: The dirty-bomb allegation first surfaced around Nov 17 and Iran denied it. The gas-price figure is Trump's claim.

items.text: US District Judge Charlotte Sweeney in Colorado held ICE officials and the administration in contempt for repeatedly re-arresting immigrants immediately after courts ordered their release, a practice the ACLU calls 'sham releases', Democracy Now reported on Nov 20. The central case involves Ramón Quintero Álvarez, a Mexican immigrant who has lived in the US for more than 30 years and was re-arrested right after leaving the Aurora ICE detention centre in late October. Any sanctions were not detailed.
items.notes: Only one outlet seen (left-leaning). Ruling date and penalties not confirmed.

items.text: On Nov 20 US District Judge Vernon Oliver, a Biden appointee, preliminarily blocked four sections of Connecticut's 2026 law SB 397. The sections would have let the state Inspector General investigate and criminally prosecute federal agents and made it a misdemeanour for officers to wear face coverings while dealing with the public. He found the provisions likely violate the Supremacy Clause because they impose conditions and penalties on federal officers, and said the Justice Department, which sued in May, is likely to win. Courts have also blocked California's ban on masked federal agents.
items.notes: This is a preliminary injunction and the case continues.

items.text: The AP reports that the Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to let the EPA cancel about $16 billion in Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund 'green bank' grants created by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. In August a divided DC Circuit panel ruled the terminations unlawful, but release of the money was paused, under a deal with the grantees, to give the justices a chance to weigh in. The petition, filed this month (docket 26-589, Climate United Fund and other nonprofits as respondents), is on the regular docket, not the emergency docket. The justices have not said whether they will take the case.
items.notes: The petition appears to date from early November (a Climate United filing on the docket is dated Nov 2), but the AP story ran Nov 19 and SCOTUSblog covered it Nov 20. Sources give the amount as $16bn, $17bn or $20bn.

items.text: The FDA published a new web page and report on shellfish harvesting in federal waters, including a sanitary survey of the federal-waters portion of the San Pedro Shelf off southern California and a letter to NOAA about Seafood Inspection Program contracts for harvesters there. Separately, Grand Strand Sandwich Company recalled lunch-box sandwiches on Nov 19 over possible Listeria contamination. The FDA's outbreak table also updated entries for a romaine-linked Salmonella outbreak and two other Salmonella outbreaks.
items.notes: This is a routine digest. No new FDA commissioner nominee was found.

items.text: During a large Russian strike on western Ukraine overnight on Nov 19–20, three Russian objects entered Polish airspace and crashed in south-east Poland. A Kh-101 cruise missile fell in a field at Nowy Lipowiec (Biłgoraj county, Lublin region), about 200–300 m from houses. Another missile fell in forest near Rudnik nad Sanem, and what was probably a jet-powered drone fell at Mołodycz (Jarosław county, both Podkarpackie). Nobody was hurt. One roof was damaged, possibly by the blast wave. Gen. Ireneusz Nowak said 11 objects threatened Polish airspace and three crossed the border, at 6:29 and 6:34 according to the BBN. The Operational Command said fighters were cleared to fire, but the conditions for doing so were not met. Defence Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz called it one of the largest such incidents since 2022. Prosecutors in Lublin are investigating.
items.thread: Russian missiles and drones over Poland
items.notes: There was early confusion over Rudnik. The Podkarpackie voivode first described the falls at Rudnik and Mołodycz as unmanned aircraft, while the defence minister spoke of a missile at Rudnik (WP live blog). The early Notes from Poland report said only 'unidentified object', and the army at first called it a 'suspected' violation.

items.text: PM Donald Tusk said it was certain that what fell in Poland came from Russia, and that it looked like an intentional provocation, not an accident. He and Defence Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz linked the timing to the coalition of the willing's KOALICJA 26.2 exercise at Nowa Dęba. Tusk spoke at length with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. Rutte called the violations clearly dangerous, said allied jets were scrambled, and said NATO will keep strengthening deterrence. He was due in Warsaw on Saturday, Nov 21. Kosiniak-Kamysz said he would ask NATO for extra forces for Eastern Sentry and for more surveillance and air defence. Macron, Czech President Pavel and Portugal expressed solidarity. No invocation of NATO Article 4 had been reported.
items.thread: Russian missiles and drones over Poland
items.notes: The outcome of Rutte's Saturday visit was not yet reported when this was researched. No Russian official response was found. The BBN said President Nawrocki had been briefed since early morning, but no presidential statement was found. Right-wing outlets (wPolityce) ran pieces blaming the government over air defence; those articles could not be opened.

items.text: The incident raised questions about civilian warnings. Government spokesman Adam Szłapka said the RCB sent a first warning of a possible threat at 2:31. A phone alert went out at 6:30, sirens sounded in Nowy Lipowiec a minute later, and the missile fell at 6:36. Some residents said warnings arrived only after the explosion. Andrzej Borowiec, wójt of Aleksandrów, said his phone alert came seconds after the impact and that outlying villages need more sirens. He added that local officials get no earlier information than ordinary citizens. Tusk said he would check the timing of the sirens and alerts.
items.thread: Russian missiles and drones over Poland
items.notes: The right-wing portal prawy.pl reported, without corroboration found, that the Rzeszów-Jasionka control tower was evacuated and civil air traffic briefly halted. That claim is not included as fact.

items.text: President Karol Nawrocki appointed Finance Minister Andrzej Domański as deputy prime minister, the fourth in Donald Tusk's government, and appointed Agnieszka Bartol minister of funds and regional policy, at a ceremony in the Presidential Palace's Column Hall. He also dismissed Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who left the government and Polska 2050 in October. Bartol, 54, is a career EU official and was Poland's ambassador to the EU. The appointments had been delayed for a month amid the President–government conflict. A presidential minister said that if it had been up to Nawrocki there would have been no promotion. Tusk wrote on X that both would work for Poland in their new roles.
items.notes: Resolves W-261105-07. Rzeczpospolita (Nov 17) described contradictory signals from the Chancellery beforehand (Bogucki vs spokesman Leśkiewicz).

items.text: Tusk said the Christmas wafer (opłatek) meeting he had proposed to President Nawrocki will not take place. He said the President had indicated they would probably not meet before the holidays and would send good wishes instead. On Nov 11 Tusk had publicly invited Nawrocki and his family to his flat in Sopot to talk 'like one Pole with another'.
items.notes: Based on Tusk's account; no Chancellery comment found.

items.text: A consortium led by FedEx completed its €7.8bn (34.5bn zł) takeover of InPost, Poland's parcel-locker and delivery company, at €15.60 a share. InPost was delisted from Euronext Amsterdam. FedEx and the US fund Advent each hold 37%, founder Rafał Brzoska's A&R Investments 16% and the Czech PPF 10%. InPost keeps its Polish headquarters, brand and operational independence, and Brzoska stays CEO. The deal was announced in February and cleared by the European Commission in August.
items.notes: No Polish government reaction reported.

items.text: The Military District Court in Warsaw overturned the acquittal of soldier Karol S. and sent his case back for retrial. He is charged with exceeding his powers by firing 12 warning shots at a group of migrants near Dubicze Cerkiewne on the Belarus border on March 25, 2024. The court said at least three shots put migrants, and fellow soldiers and Border Guard officers, at direct risk of death or serious injury. The charge carries up to three years in prison. The garrison court in Lublin had acquitted him.
items.notes: Politically sensitive: the right has campaigned for soldiers prosecuted over border incidents. No reaction found yet.

items.text: The Energy Minister set maximum fuel prices for Saturday to Monday (Nov 21–23): 5.90 zł a litre for 95 petrol, 6.55 zł for 98 petrol and 7.39 zł for diesel, under the daily price-cap scheme.
items.notes: Figures come from the WNP headline only. The article would not load, and the date (Nov 20) is inferred from the article ID sequence, so check it before relying on it.
